subject: Geography
title: Practical Relief and Contours
outline: Methods of representing relief on maps
Contours, contour interval and vertical exaggeration
Recognition of relief features from contour patterns
Relationship between relief, drainage, settlement and landuse
Interpretation of relief for human activities

modules.title: Representing Relief and Reading Contours
modules.html:
Methods of Showing Relief

  1. Contours - lines joining points of equal height above sea level; the most accurate and most widely used method.
  2. Spot heights and trigonometrical stations - exact heights at a point.
  3. Hachures - short lines drawn down the slope; thick and close for steep slopes.
  4. Layer (hypsometric) tinting - colour bands for height ranges: green lowlands, yellow and brown uplands, purple or white for very high land.
  5. Hill shading and form lines - pictorial impressions of relief.

Contour Rules

  • Contours never cross one another, except at an overhanging cliff.
  • Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope; widely spaced contours indicate a gentle slope.
  • Evenly spaced contours indicate a uniform slope.
  • V-shaped contours pointing upstream indicate a valley; rounded contours pointing downhill indicate a spur.
  • Closed contours with increasing values represent a hill; with hachured inward ticks they represent a depression.

Recognising Relief Features

FeatureContour pattern
Conical hillSmall evenly spaced concentric rings
RidgeElongated concentric contours with a narrow crest
PlateauWidely spaced contours enclosing a large flat summit, steep at the edges
Escarpment (cuesta)Contours close on one side (scarp) and far apart on the other (dip slope)
Col / saddleA gap between two areas of high ground
ValleyV-shaped contours pointing to higher ground, often with a river
Convex slopeContours far apart at the top, closer at the base
Concave slopeContours close at the top, wider at the base

Gradient

Gradient compares vertical rise with horizontal distance, both in the same units:

$$\text{Gradient} = \frac{\text{Vertical interval (V.I.)}}{\text{Horizontal equivalent (H.E.)}} = 1 \text{ in } n$$

Both measurements must be converted to metres before the ratio is simplified.

examples.q: On a 1:50,000 map, a hill top of 420 m lies 4 cm from a point at 120 m. Calculate the gradient.
examples.a: Vertical interval \(=420-120 = 300\text{ m}\). Horizontal equivalent: 1 cm = 0.5 km, so \(4\text{ cm} = 2\text{ km} = 2000\text{ m}\). Gradient \(= \dfrac{300}{2000} = \dfrac{1}{6.67}\), i.e. approximately 1 in 6.7.

examples.q: How can you tell an escarpment from a ridge on a contour map?
examples.a: An escarpment (cuesta) is asymmetrical: contours are very close together on one side, showing the steep scarp face, and widely spaced on the other, showing the gentle dip slope. A ridge is a narrow elongated upland whose contours are fairly close on both flanks, giving a roughly symmetrical cross-profile with a well-defined crest line.

modules.title: Cross-Sections, Vertical Exaggeration and Intervisibility
modules.html:
Drawing a Cross-Section

  1. Join the two given points with a straight line and lay the edge of a strip of paper along it.
  2. Mark on the paper every point where a contour, river, road or railway crosses, and write its value.
  3. Draw a horizontal base line of the same length and a vertical axis with a suitable vertical scale, e.g. 1 cm to 100 m.
  4. Transfer each mark, plot its height, and join the points with a smooth free-hand curve.
  5. Title the section, state both scales and the vertical exaggeration, and annotate the features.

Vertical Exaggeration

Because relief is small compared with horizontal distance, the vertical scale is exaggerated:

$$\text{V.E.} = \frac{\text{Vertical scale}}{\text{Horizontal scale}}$$

Both scales must first be expressed as representative fractions with the same units. Exaggeration makes relief clearer, but too much of it produces unnaturally steep and misleading slopes.

Intervisibility

Two points are intervisible if an unbroken line of sight can be drawn between them on the cross-section. Visibility is obstructed by intervening higher ground, a convex slope, a ridge, thick forest or tall buildings, but is aided by concave slopes, uniform slopes falling away from the observer and greater observer height.

Drainage Interpretation

On a topographical map, note the main river and its tributaries, the drainage pattern and density, the direction of flow (V-shaped contours point upstream; tributaries join at acute angles pointing downstream), and features such as rapids, swamps, deltas or braiding. High drainage density suggests impermeable rock and heavy rainfall; low density suggests permeable rock such as limestone or sand.

Relief, Drainage, Settlement and Landuse

Relief and drainage influence human activity: settlements avoid steep slopes and flood plains, concentrating on gentle terraces, dry points and river confluences; roads and railways follow valleys, cols and gentle gradients; farming occupies fertile lowlands and terraces; forestry and grazing occupy steep upland slopes; and reservoirs are sited in narrow valleys with resistant rock.

examples.q: A cross-section has a horizontal scale of 1:50,000 and a vertical scale of 1 cm to 100 m. Calculate the vertical exaggeration.
examples.a: Vertical scale as an R.F.: \(100\text{ m} = 10{,}000\text{ cm}\), so \(1{:}10{,}000\). Then \(\text{V.E.} = \dfrac{1/10{,}000}{1/50{,}000} = \dfrac{50{,}000}{10{,}000} = 5\). The vertical scale is exaggerated 5 times.

examples.q: State three reasons why two points on a map may not be intervisible.
examples.a: (i) A hill, ridge or spur of greater height stands between them and blocks the line of sight; (ii) the intervening slope is convex, so the ground bulges above the straight line joining the two points; (iii) obstacles such as dense forest, plantations or tall buildings lie in the line of sight. A cross-section drawn between the points confirms the obstruction.

quiz.q: Contours are lines joining places of equal
quiz.solution: Isohyets join rainfall, isotherms temperature; contours join equal heights.
The height changes rapidly over a short horizontal distance.

quiz.q: The method of showing relief using colour bands for height ranges is called
quiz.solution: Layer or hypsometric tinting uses green, yellow, brown and purple bands.

quiz.q: The vertical difference in height between two successive contours is the
quiz.solution: It is stated in the map margin, commonly 30 m or 50 m.

quiz.q: A gap between two hills through which a road may pass is a
quiz.solution: A col or saddle is a low point on a ridge between two summits.

quiz.q: V-shaped contours pointing towards higher ground indicate
quiz.solution: The V opens downstream, so the apex points upstream to higher land.

quiz.q: An escarpment is recognised on a map by contours that are
options: close on one side and wide on the other
quiz.solution: The steep scarp face contrasts with the gentle dip slope.

quiz.q: If the vertical interval is 200 m and the horizontal equivalent is 4,000 m, the gradient is
Vertical exaggeration is obtained by dividing the
options: horizontal scale by the vertical scale
vertical scale by the horizontal scale
quiz.solution: Both scales must be expressed as representative fractions first.

quiz.q: With a horizontal scale of 1:100,000 and a vertical scale of 1 cm to 200 m, the vertical exaggeration is
Two points are said to be intervisible when
options: they lie at the same height
an unbroken line of sight joins them
they are on the same contour
quiz.solution: A cross-section is drawn to test whether the sight line is blocked.

quiz.q: A convex slope is shown by contours that are
options: close at the top and wide at the base
wide at the top and close at the base
quiz.solution: The slope steepens downhill, so contours crowd near the base.

quiz.q: On a map, a river's direction of flow can be deduced from
options: the V of contours and the angle of tributary junctions
quiz.solution: Tributaries join at acute angles pointing downstream.

quiz.q: A drainage pattern with a very high density usually suggests
quiz.solution: Impermeable rocks encourage surface run-off and many channels.

quiz.q: Settlements on a topographical map are commonly sited
options: along flood plains subject to annual flooding
at dry points near water supply and gentle land
quiz.solution: People choose sites with water nearby but safe from flooding, on land easy to build on.

quiz.q: Which relief feature is shown by widely spaced contours enclosing a large flat summit with steep edges?
quiz.solution: A plateau is an extensive elevated flat land bounded by steep slopes.

options: short lines drawn along the direction of slope
quiz.solution: Thick, closely drawn hachures indicate steep slopes.
